Prevention: Shoot and fruit borer is a small moth which caterpillar bore and fed on plant parts.
Collect and destroy (burn or bury) all crop residues from the previous season.
Establish maize trap barriers around eggplant plots 15 days before eggplant transplanting.
Use tolerant varieties; round-shaped fruit bearing varieties have a higher tolerance to borer pest (e.g.
Raise seedlings far away from sources of infestation (old eggplant fields, eggplant stubble).
Grow seedlings under nylon netting to prevent moths from laying eggs on the plants.
Intercrop with coriander or fennel to reduce pest infestation.
Conserve natural enemies by avoiding broad spectrum insecticides and providing suitable habitat.
Harrow the field to expose larvae to sunlight to kill them.
Monitoring: Start monitoring for borers at the vegetative stage:
Look for drooping tender shoots and wilting.
Observe crops for small exit holes below the calyx of fruits and the presence of larvae inside damaged fruit and shoots.
At crop fruiting stage, look for holes filled with insect excretions.
Adult moth wingspan between 18-24 mm, with white wings and characteristic brown 'heart' patterns.
Larvae are reddish-translucent in colour and can grow up to 15 mm long.
Follow control actions if 2% of plants or a minimum of 1% of fruit show symptoms.
Direct Control: Practice good farm sanitation, burn infested plant materials or bury 3 ft deep into the ground.
Azatrol with 1 part water, spray at 7-10 day intervals.
Separate damaged pods during harvest and bury or burn to kill larvae.
Use light traps to capture adult moths at night.
Remove and destroy infested shoots (readily visible as dry tip of branches).
Burn, shred into tiny pieces or bury attacked shoots at least 20 cm in the soil.
Cut once a week until harvest.
Need to be done at community level.
